title: Physics: Mechanics for Biomedical Engineers
description: Kinematics, forces, energy, momentum, rotation, and material response taught through free-body diagrams and experimental checks.

modifications: Expanded the week-1 kinematics and force-balance reading with position, velocity and acceleration distinctions; free-body diagram boundaries; Newton's second law; axis-resolved incline forces; and unit and limiting-case checks. Clarified both objectives and linked them to outcomes 1, 2 and 4.

Expanded the week-4 work, energy and power reading with the work–energy theorem, gravitational and spring potential energy, energy accounting for a drop, conservative and dissipative transfers, and power units. Clarified both objectives and linked them to outcomes 2 and 4.

Expanded the week-6 momentum, collisions and impulse reading with signed momentum, external-impulse conditions, force–time area, momentum change and the distinction between momentum and kinetic-energy conservation. Clarified both objectives and linked them to outcomes 2 and 4.

Expanded week 9 with perpendicular moment arms, signed planar torque, moments about a common axis, engineering stress and strain, small-strain modulus calculations, dimensional checks, and model limits. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 3 and 4.

Added an original variable-mass momentum lesson deriving momentum flux for inflow and outflow, applying it to an ideal rocket and a mass-capturing cart, and stating system/frame assumptions; added eight formative items and four cards with synthetic values. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

prerequisites.statement: Algebra and trigonometry; calculus taken concurrently

outcomes.description: Build a free-body diagram with consistent axes.
Apply conservation laws and Newton's laws.
Quantify torque, angular momentum, and rotational energy.
Check mechanical predictions against units and limiting cases.

lesson_objectives.description: Apply Newton's second law to a defined system and calculate acceleration from its net force and mass.
Draw a force balance with stated axes and resolve gravity and support forces on a frictionless incline.
Calculate translational kinetic energy and relate net work to its change.
Compare gravitational potential energy with final kinetic energy and interpret the difference within a stated model.
Apply signed momentum conservation to a one-dimensional sticking collision when external impulse is negligible.
Calculate impulse as signed area under a force–time curve and relate it to momentum change with units.
Calculate the magnitude and sign of torque about a stated axis using force direction and the perpendicular moment arm.
Calculate engineering stress, strain and a declared small-strain elastic modulus; check units and model limits.
Calculate impact speed and momentum from a drop height using energy conservation.
Compute the average stopping force from impulse (momentum change over time) and from work–energy (kinetic energy over stopping distance).
Check predictions against units and limiting cases, and evaluate what an average force does and does not tell you about peak loads.
Convert rotation rate to angular velocity and compute centripetal acceleration and relative centrifugal force, and find the speed for a target force.
Calculate a rotor's moment of inertia, rotational kinetic energy, angular momentum and the torque needed for a given spin-up.
Quantify the rotating force from a mass imbalance and check results with units and limiting cases.
Differentiate a position vector and distinguish speed from velocity.
Calculate a constrained projectile event in consistent axes.
Check frame, sampling and event-domain assumptions.
Identify body-specific forces, contact and consistent axes.
Apply static-friction inequalities and sliding force balances.
Distinguish contact force, net force and third-law partners.
Apply system momentum balance and distinguish kinetic energy loss.
Calculate impulse and variable-force work with explicit boundaries.
Qualify force averages and contact/gravity assumptions.
Compute torque and axis-specific inertia.
Relate angular momentum, energy and constrained rolling speed.
Check angular and rolling constraint assumptions.
Calculate oscillator frequencies and impose initial conditions.
Relate envelope decay to mechanical energy and dissipation.
Check parameter inference and damping-regime limits.
Calculate stress, strain and defined modulus with consistent geometry.
Apply a supplied scalar time-dependent constitutive law.
Evaluate measurement and orientation-model scope.
Distinguish baseline, machine compliance and specimen compliance.
Recover specimen stiffness and modulus from a supplied reference.
Evaluate conditional material inference and metadata needs.
Summarize raw displacement reports and distinguish baseline from compliance.
Recover machine compliance and specimen stiffness using a supplied reference.
Evaluate positive-compliance feasibility and conditional orientation comparisons.
Choose a system and inertial frame and identify momentum carried by incoming and outgoing mass.
Apply a one-dimensional mass-flow momentum balance to a rocket or a body that captures material, using consistent signs and velocity frames.
Derive and use the ideal constant-exhaust-speed rocket velocity increment and evaluate its assumptions with units and limiting cases.
Apply Newton's law of universal gravitation, including the shell result, to find the gravitational force and field strength at a distance from a spherical body.
Calculate the speed and period of a circular orbit, apply Kepler's third law for circular orbits, and find the radius for a given period.
Use U = −GMm/r to calculate orbital energy, the energy to reach an orbit and the escape speed, and explain when mgh is an adequate approximation.
Solve coupled translational and rotational force balances.
Cross-check a coupled constraint with rotational and energy ledgers.
Test an inertia limit without discarding the constraint model.
Identify when a coupled-motion solution stops applying.
Solve the slip event before imposing rolling.
Close endpoint and contact-power mechanical-energy balances.
Analyze overspin without equating friction with center deceleration.
Evaluate contact power and choose the correct post-event law.
Compare closed-event and growing-body momentum/energy ledgers.
Close external work, changing kinetic energy and capture loss.
Solve a distinct constrained force/torque system.
Verify endpoint kinematics and rotational energy before the boundary event.
Locate a new slip event and its rolling state.
Check overspin power and an event-aware simulation interpretation.
Distinguish numerical energy growth from a physical driving mechanism.
Compare method artifacts with a separately declared damping law.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. Week 6 now links the fixed-mass momentum/impulse foundation to a variable-mass momentum and mass-flow lesson; week 10 pairs centrifuge circular motion with universal gravitation and circular orbits; week 14 remains a synthetic machine-compliance/orientation lab. Weeks 11–12 add an optional rotor trade-off project with rehearsal practice and milestone self-checks. All activities are open, ungraded practice. There are no graded homework sets, exams or graded project, and workload has not been measured, so this schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

weeks.title: Momentum, collisions, impulse, and variable-mass flow
Impact forces: impulse, work–energy and why stopping more slowly protects tissue
Uniform circular motion: an ideal centrifuge model, universal gravitation and circular orbits
Oscillations, damping and energy balance; optional rotor trade-off project

workload.basis: Not measured. Legacy nominal credit and display-time labels are not retained as workload estimates.

lessons.title: Kinematics and force balance
lessons.worked_example: A 3 kg cart under a 12 N net horizontal force accelerates at 4 m/s². A 10 kg block on a frictionless 30° incline accelerates at g sin(30°)=4.905 m/s² and has normal force mg cos(30°)≈84.96 N. A 0.20 kg package accelerating upward at 2 m/s² requires tension 0.20(9.81+2)=2.36 N.

lessons.title: Work, energy, and power
lessons.worked_example: A 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s has 9 J of translational kinetic energy. For the preserved drop, initial mgh=98.1 J and final translational kinetic energy is 64.0 J, leaving a 34.1 J mechanical-energy difference under the stated model. A 200 N/m spring compressed 0.05 m stores 0.25 J.

lessons.title: Momentum, collisions, and impulse
lessons.worked_example: A 0.10 kg cart moving at +5 m/s sticks to a stationary 0.40 kg cart, giving final speed +1.0 m/s when external impulse is negligible. A triangular 200 N pulse lasting 0.020 s has impulse +2.0 N·s. A 0.15 kg ball changing velocity from +8 to −4 m/s receives impulse −1.8 N·s.

lessons.title: Rotation, torque, and material response
lessons.worked_example: A 30 N downward force applied 0.20 m from a hinge at a perpendicular moment arm gives a torque magnitude of 6 N·m. If counterclockwise is positive, the downward force turns clockwise, so τz = −6 N·m. The sign records direction, while the requested magnitude is positive; force times moment arm gives N·m.

lessons.title: Impact forces: impulse, work–energy and why stopping more slowly protects tissue
lessons.worked_example: A 0.5 m drop gives 3.13 m/s; a 70 kg body then has 219.2 kg·m/s and 343.4 J; stopping in 10 ms needs 21925 N on average, in 50 ms 4385 N, and over 2 cm of padding 17168 N.

lessons.title: Uniform circular motion and rigid-body rotation: an ideal centrifuge model
lessons.worked_example: At 3000 rpm, a point at 0.10 m has inward acceleration 9,870 m/s²; an ideal 2 kg, 0.12 m disk has 711 J of rotational energy; a 1 g point-mass imbalance corresponds to a 9.87 N rotating support load.

modules.title: Universal gravitation, circular orbits and orbital energy

lessons.title: Universal gravitation, circular orbits and orbital energy
lessons.worked_example: Around a synthetic planet with GM = 4.0 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², a 500 kg satellite at r = 8.0 × 10⁶ m moves at 7.07 km/s with period 7107 s; its energy is −1.25 × 10¹⁰ J, placing it there from rest on the surface takes 1.88 × 10¹⁰ J, and escape from that radius needs 10.0 km/s.

lessons.title: Vector kinematics, frames and constraints
lessons.worked_example: Differentiate each polynomial component before inserting t=2, giving velocity (6,1) and acceleration (2,1). Compute speed by the vector norm and compare it with average displacement divided by two seconds. In the separate projectile model, impose the landing condition y=0, retain the positive-time root and multiply by horizontal speed for range. At the apex, set only v_y to zero. Finally subtract the supplied observer velocity for the constant-frame comparison.

lessons.title: Free-body diagrams, contact and friction
lessons.worked_example: For the level block, calculate N=19.62 and the static limit 7.848 N. Compare the required friction under a 6 N push with that limit before selecting a model. For 8 N and rightward sliding, use kinetic friction 3.924 and net force 4.076. In the inclined example, project weight, test the static inequality and then compute the downhill acceleration. Finally distinguish tension 21.62 N from the 2 N net force in the suspended example.

lessons.title: Work, momentum and system boundaries
lessons.worked_example: Sum signed initial momenta for the sticking pair, divide by total mass and check the final momentum. Calculate kinetic energies separately and retain the 0.96 J reduction as a mechanical-energy change. For the vertical stop, find net impulse from Δp, then add back the opposing gravitational contribution to recover contact impulse. For the separate variable-force particle, integrate in position for 21 J and solve the positive speed from kinetic energy.

lessons.title: Torque, angular momentum and rolling
lessons.worked_example: Use the cross product component 0.20×30−0.10×10 for torque +5.0. Calculate I from the supplied disk geometry, then obtain α, rotational energy and angular momentum with their distinct units and speed dependence. For the separate cylinder, impose v=Rω and include both energy terms before solving for center speed. Finally check whether the required static friction fits the bound instead of assuming rolling without slip automatically.

lessons.title: Oscillations, damping and energy balance
lessons.worked_example: Calculate ω₀=10 and δ=0.80, confirm the underdamped inequality and obtain ω_d from their squared difference. Divide 2π by ω_d for period and ln2 by δ for envelope half-time. Use the zero-velocity initial condition to retain the sine term. Independently compute initial energy 0.0100 J and verify that any integrated trajectory loses exactly the modeled drag energy. Compare c with 10 N·s/m before deciding which regime formula applies.

modules.title: Stress, strain, orientation and time dependence

lessons.title: Stress, strain, orientation and time dependence
lessons.worked_example: Divide 10 N by 2.0×10⁻⁶ m² for 5 MPa, then divide 0.00020 by 0.020 for strain 0.010 and form 500 MPa. For the independent spring–dashpot construction, add Eε and η times strain rate for 2500 Pa. Under the stipulated constant stress, solve the first-order balance for τ=0.50 and limiting strain 0.030, then evaluate its fraction at one time constant. Keep geometry-based stiffness, orientation and time-dependent model parameters distinct.

modules.title: Machine compliance, calibration and model inference

lessons.title: Machine compliance, calibration and model inference
lessons.worked_example: At 0.30 N, add offset 2.0 mm, machine elongation 0.30 mm and specimen elongation 0.30 mm for reported 2.60 mm. Fit total compliance independently of the intercept, subtract the known reference contribution to obtain machine compliance and remove it before inversion. Convert corrected 1000 N/m to 20 MPa with the stated geometry, versus apparent 10 MPa. In the separate lab orientation pair, recover the two-to-one corrected ratio while preserving the shared reporting terms.

modules.title: Virtual lab 1: machine compliance and orientation-dependent stiffness

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: machine compliance and orientation-dependent stiffness
lessons.worked_example: Synthetic reference slope 0.5 mm/N identifies machine compliance under an ideal zero-compliance reference. Corrected specimen slopes give stiffnesses 2000 and 1000 N/m; apparent stiffness ratio 1.5 becomes corrected ratio 2 with matched geometry.

modules.title: Variable-mass momentum and continuous mass transfer

lessons.title: Variable-mass momentum and continuous mass transfer
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic rocket with m0=600 kg, mf=450 kg and constant relative exhaust speed 800 m/s has an ideal external-force-free velocity increment 800 ln(4/3)=230.1 m/s; a 20 kg cart at 10 m/s that retains 5 kg at rest instead slows to 8.0 m/s.

lessons.title: Rotor trade-off project guide: speed, rotational energy and imbalance at a shared target (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For an invented 2.0 kg disk of radius 0.050 m at 1,000 × g, ω²r = 9,810 m/s² gives ω² = 196,200 rad²/s², about 442.9 rad/s or 4,230 rpm. Then I = ½MR² = 0.0025 kg·m², K = ½Iω² = 245.25 J, and a 0.0002 kg point imbalance at the rim needs F = mω²r ≈ 1.962 N.

lessons.title: Massive pulleys and coupled constraints
lessons.worked_example: The reflected pulley inertia is two kilograms, making effective total mass ten kilograms. Acceleration is 1.962 m/s². The separate mass balances give T1=35.316 N and T2=39.24 N; their difference accelerates the massive pulley rather than vanishing.

modules.title: Sliding to rolling: contact velocity, torque and power

lessons.title: Sliding to rolling: contact velocity, torque and power
lessons.worked_example: The initial slip is three meters per second. It decreases at mu g(1+1/beta)=5.886 m/s², reaching zero at about 0.509684 s. The center speed is two meters per second and clockwise angular speed twenty rad/s. Continue with the new rolling phase rather than the old kinetic force.

modules.title: Assignment 1: impulse, capture and system boundaries

lessons.title: Assignment 1: impulse, capture and system boundaries
lessons.worked_example: The collision retains momentum 0.4 kg m/s and ends at 0.2 m/s; kinetic energy drops from 2.2 to 0.04 J. For capture from rest with no external force, growing-body momentum stays six kg m/s, so at mass four kilograms the velocity is 1.5 m/s and kinetic energy 4.5 J. Momentum and energy conservation are separate conditions.

lessons.title: Assignment 2: coupled motion and constraints
lessons.worked_example: Reflected inertia is two kilograms, yielding effective total mass ten. The force/torque system gives a=3.924 m/s², T1=27.468 N and T2=35.316 N. Their 7.848 N difference provides the pulley torque required by alpha=a/R. This check depends on the declared phase and its explicit mechanical assumptions.

lessons.title: Assignment 3: sliding-to-rolling transition study
lessons.worked_example: Slip changes at mu g(1+1/0.4)=8.58375 m/s², giving transition time about 0.32619776 s. The rolling speed is 2 m/s and spin is 2/0.12 rad/s. Initial energy 5.88 J falls to 4.2 J, a loss of 1.68 J under the stipulated contact model.

modules.title: Assignment 4: oscillator simulation and model verification

lessons.title: Assignment 4: oscillator simulation and model verification
lessons.worked_example: Old-state Euler gives x1=0.1 and v1=−0.04. Its energy is 0.5×0.04²+0.5×4×0.1²=0.0208 J, above the exact initial/conserved 0.02 J. This method’s numerical growth factor is 1+omega0²h², not evidence that a passive undamped spring adds energy. This check depends on the declared phase and its explicit mechanical assumptions.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added an original lesson on impact forces (impulse, work–energy, average versus peak force and scaling checks) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on centrifuge rotation (relative centrifugal force, moment of inertia, rotational energy, torque and imbalance) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added seven original lessons on vector/frame kinematics, contact/friction, work/momentum boundaries, rotation/rolling, damping/energy, scalar time-dependent materials and machine-compliance inference; one synthetic orientation/compliance lab and a proposed weekly schedule. Developed with Codex assistance. Still partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded week 1 with kinematics, force diagrams, Newton's second law, force components on a frictionless incline, and unit and limiting-case checks. Clarified both objectives and mapped them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 1, 2 and 4. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged. Compact prototype readings remain in weeks 4, 6 and 9; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded week 4 with kinetic energy, the work–energy theorem, gravitational and spring potential energy, mechanical-energy differences, conservative and dissipative transfers, and power. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 2 and 4. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged. Compact prototype readings remain in weeks 6 and 9; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded week 6 with signed momentum, external-impulse conditions for conservation, force–time area, impulse–momentum balance, and the distinction between momentum and kinetic-energy conservation. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 2 and 4. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged. One compact prototype reading remains in week 9; the course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Expanded week 9 with perpendicular moment arms, signed torque, stress and strain definitions, small-strain modulus calculations, and explicit model limits. Clarified both objectives and mapped them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 3 and 4. Added one OpenStax torque reference and reused the registered stress/strain section. Existing question IDs, prompts, answer keys and cards are unchanged; all 13 readings now have substantive instruction beside the synthetic data lab. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an inactive, ungraded synthetic rotor trade-off portfolio comparing equal-RCF speed, idealized disk inertia and energy, and point-imbalance force; linked it from the syllabus while keeping platform activation off. Existing lessons, practice items, keys and cards are unchanged. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only; invented values are not an operating specification.

Rebounded the centrifuge reading to stipulated circular-motion and rigid-body models; removed unsupported sedimentation-time, temperature and equipment-protocol claims, clarified the acceleration-ratio meaning of RCF, and reframed its example and practice item. Added a direct 8.01SC syllabus comparator. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added an original week-6 variable-mass momentum lesson deriving inflow/outflow momentum flux, a signed rocket equation and a retained-mass capture example. Eight formative items and four cards use synthetic values. Compared with undergraduate MIT OCW 8.01SC Fall 2016 Week 6 continuous mass transfer and its rocket/recoil scope; no source material was imported. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Extended the bounded week-10 circular-motion and rotation lesson with a rotating-frame description: the centrifugal pseudo-force that balances the real inward force for a point at rest on the rotor, agreement of both frames on the measurable support force, the Coriolis term the lesson does not need, and a rule against mixing frames in one free-body diagram. The lesson now uses the standard worked-example and limits headings. No item, key or card changed. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Grouped an original universal-gravitation and circular-orbit reading with the week-10 circular-motion lesson: the inverse-square law and shell result, local field strength, orbital speed and period, Kepler's third law for circular orbits, gravitational potential energy, orbital energy and escape speed. Added three objectives, eleven formative items and four cards, with no week added, and corrected stale limitation counts (fourteen readings and 66 numeric items before this release, not thirteen and 63). The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Made the planned rotor trade-off project usable by learners as ungraded practice. Week 11 gains an optional project guide with the project's candidates and tasks, a worked single-rotor example, two synthetic rehearsal candidates and 4 open rehearsal practice items; five project milestones are Case studio self-checks with a week-12 project record. The draft's table now lists candidate C's 0.6 kg disk mass, matching its CSV and reference calculations, and the project table becomes a learner resource. The compliance lab's dataset link now points to the package-pinned CSV instead of a mutable repository URL. The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added original massive-pulley/constraint and slip-to-roll/contact-power foundations, four connected momentum/energy/constraint/contact/simulation assignments, sixteen checkpoint items/cards and an analytic synthetic oscillator table. Distinguishes tension/torque coupling, contact-event laws and physical versus numerical energy changes. Preserves the rotor project and compliance lab; all models are synthetic, partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: The core and new coupled/contact readings have substantive instruction beside one synthetic data lab; this is not a full university semester.

The proposed 14-week sequence is unmeasured and unreviewed. Graded homework, exams, a full laboratory sequence and an active graded cumulative project remain absent. An optional rotor trade-off project guide with rehearsal practice and Case studio milestone self-checks (weeks 11–12) is ungraded practice; the rotor portfolio itself remains an inactive authoring draft.

All parameters and reports are synthetic; selected point-particle, rigid-body, contact and scalar material models provide no real equipment or specimen-testing procedure. In particular, ω²r and RCF determine acceleration only; they do not predict sedimentation or justify a speed, time or temperature protocol.
Public keys and feedback remain formative authoring specifications; practice points are not course grades.
Subject-matter, accessibility and workload review remain outstanding; the original text free-body diagram has a verbal description but no assistive-technology review.
Fifteen primary OpenStax University Physics Volume 1 sections are registered as link-only references; no teaching prose, problem, figure or dataset was imported.

The new variable-mass lesson is a one-dimensional point-body model with uniform stream velocities and stated external forces. It does not cover engine thermodynamics, pressure thrust, multidimensional flow, vehicle control or real propulsion design.

The rotor trade-off project is optional and ungraded. Its five milestones are Case studio self-checks whose private drafts are never submitted or scored; the rehearsal practice uses separate invented candidates at a different target, and no software check evaluates a learner's project calculations or written comparison. Milestone weeks are planning suggestions, not measured workload or deadlines.

Two new selected coupled-constraint/contact-power foundations and four open report/simulation assignments deepen forces, momentum/energy, rolling and oscillator verification. Browser checkpoints do not evaluate diagrams, written arguments, implementations or a real apparatus. General three-dimensional rigid-body/contact, deformable rope/traction/impact characterization and measured laboratory work remain beyond these models. Workload, scientific review and broader coursework/laboratory depth remain open.
Of the 126 numerical answers, 8 require units, 52 check significant figures and 0 check dimensions. New continuous checkpoint quantities request three significant figures in the stated scales.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, complete laboratory sequence, cumulative graded project, measured workload and qualified human review remain outstanding.
The fictional rotor trade-off portfolio is an inactive, ungraded paper-exercise draft and is not activated or mapped to course completion.
A full continuum/control-volume treatment of distributed momentum transport, propulsion design and snowplow or vehicle engineering applications remains outside this bounded lesson.
